newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU finance ministers strike cautious note on lira.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers strike cautious note on lira.

text.p: European Union finance ministers on Monday applauded the Finnish markka's smooth entry into the exchange rate mechanism (ERM), but trod cautiously around the question of the Italian lira's future membership.

While issues relating to the ERM or monetary union were not formally on the agenda, EU ministers were deluged with questions on what Finland's entry meant for countries like Italy, Britain and Sweden, which remain outside the grid.
Regarding Italy, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told reporters after the ministerial gathering that the lira's re-entry would require careful consideration.
"To be hasty on the re-entry (of the lira) would mean to take a risk...which would cause harm to the Italian and European monetary authorities," Arthuis said.
He added that the lira's central parity rate should be "durable, equitable and sustainable," a position closely mirroring that of Germany's Bundesbank.
Other EU monetary officials envisaged an extraordinary situation where finance ministers would have to hold a special meeting to actually bring the lira back into the ERM.
Both the lira and sterling were ejected from the ERM in September 1992 during a crisis which nearly led to its collapse.
"I think this will have to be taken at the ministerial level," said one senior EU official.
Typically, decisions on the entry of a currency into the ERM are taken by the EU's monetary committee, a group of national treasury and central bank officials.
Italy has said it wants the lira to return to the ERM as soon as possible in order to bolster its credentials for acceptance into monetary union in 1999.
But debate over the ERM and whether membership is actually mandatory in order to qualify for a single currency has reached a new level of intensity with Finland's entry.

The Finnish markka became the 11th of 15 EU currencies in the ERM on Monday following a decision on Saturday in Brussels by the EU's monetary committee. It will trade at a central rate of 3.04 to the German mark.
The move was seen as giving a boost to EU plans for a single currency in 1999.

While the Maastricht treaty clearly states that an aspiring candidate for monetary union must reside within the ERM two years prior to the decision on which countries qualify -- early 1998 -- some countries have argued that the criterion no longer applies given the crisis in 1992.
Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto told a news conference that it became clear to him last spring that ERM membership was necessary.
"During last spring it became more and more obvious ERM membership is a criterion for the third stage of monetary union," Niinisto said.
"One could very clearly see that if in 1998 some some would say it was not necessary to belong to ERM1, then what is left of ERM2," he added.

At an informal meeting of EU finance ministers and central bankers in Verona last April there was broad agreement on the need for a revamped ERM that would link the single currency to those not participating in monetary union at the start.

While at the strong urging of Britain it was agreed the new currency system should be voluntary, Niinisto said there was a strong desire among most countries to have non-participants take part in the currency grid.
